note.note:
Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old male presented with 3-day history of moderate, self-limiting diarrhea without red flag features; clinical impression is acute viral gastroenteritis.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Diarrhea for approximately 3 days; frequency 4–5 times per day.
- Symptom timeline: Onset 3 days ago; variable stool consistency (sometimes watery, sometimes loose).
- Associated symptoms: Mild abdominal pain, single episode of vomiting, mild loss of appetite, possible mild fever (not prominent), no blood or mucus in stool.
- Pertinent negatives: No recent travel, no unusual food exposures, no significant fever, no blood/mucus in stool, no chronic GI symptoms, no dehydration (denied by clinician observation).
- Past medical history: Asthma (possibly ongoing).
- Allergies: None reported.
- Medications: Uses a yellow inhaler (name possibly miscommunicated as "Laxepro"/"Lexapro", likely an asthma inhaler); no other medications mentioned.
- Family history: Father died of bowel cancer at age 62; had hypertension.
- Social and preventive health: No recent travel, no dietary change, no social risk factors mentioned.

Examination:
- General appearance: Not dehydrated per virtual/clinical observation.
- No physical exam or vital sign abnormalities documented.
- No description of appearance beyond hydration status.

Impression:
- Most likely diagnosis: Acute viral gastroenteritis.
    - Supported by acute onset, short symptom duration, watery/loose stools, mild abdominal pain, mild/absent fever, self-limited course, absence of alarming features (no blood/mucus, maintained hydration).
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (less likely): Considered due to similar presentation; lack of severe symptoms or risk factors makes this less probable.
- Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (unlikely): Family history of bowel cancer, but no red flag symptoms (no chronicity, bleeding, or mucus), and no previous similar episodes.
- Colorectal malignancy (very unlikely): Not supported by acute onset, age, absence of alarm features; relevant only due to family history.

Plan:
- Supportive care with emphasis on hydration (continue drinking plenty of fluids).
- Soft diet recommended: Avoid dairy, fish, meat, eggs initially; advised to eat simple foods (crackers, toast, jam, mashed vegetables).
    - Gradual reintroduction of more complex foods (meat/eggs/fish) after 48 hours without diarrhea.
    - Consider yoghurt as a probiotic; avoid milk.
- Over-the-counter oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) recommended to replace lost salts.
- Red flags: Return for evaluation if diarrhea lasts more than one week, if blood appears in stool, if frequency increases to 6–8 times/day, or if unable to maintain oral intake or symptoms worsen.
- If red flags present, stool sample and further investigation may be needed.
- Patient encouraged to re-consult or seek urgent care if concerned.

Quality checks

● Missing or clinically expected elements:
    - Vitals not documented (e.g., temperature, heart rate).
    - Further detail on medications and inhaler type not clarified.
    - No examination beyond hydration status.
    - No explicit follow-up timeframe arranged.
    - Social/occupational risk factors not explored.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
    - None significant; both agree on most likely diagnosis and absence of features for alternative causes.
    - Minor confusion noted in transcript about inhaler name (possible miscommunication).
● Transcript quality:
    - Sufficient to establish diagnosis and plan, but mildly incomplete for full medication and exam details.
    - Some ambiguity regarding inhaler name and description.
    - Otherwise clear and well-structured.
